subject: mathematics

sections.title: Perimeter of a Shape
sections.think_reflect: Asks the student to see the connection between finding the perimeter of a circle and the opening question about the staggered lanes of a 400 m athletics track.

sections.title: Perimeter of a Circle — The C/D Ratio
Length of an Arc of a Circle
sections.think_reflect: Asks the student to use the schematic 400 m track to find the difference in radius between the first and second lanes, compute the stagger the second-lane runner needs, and decide whether the same stagger applies between the second and third lanes.

sections.title: Problems, Puzzles, and Paradoxes on Perimeter
Area of a Parallelogram
sections.think_reflect: Asks the student to repair the cut-and-rearrange argument when the parallelogram is so 'thin' that the foot of the perpendicular falls outside the base, and to decide whether the area of a parallelogram can be found from its side lengths alone.

sections.title: Area of a Triangle
sections.think_reflect: Asks the student whether the two equal-area triangles formed by a median can actually be cut into pieces and rearranged to cover each other, whether any two equal-area polygons are always related by such a dissection, and which of the rectangles of perimeter 40 units has the largest and the smallest area.

sections.title: Squaring a Rectangle
sections.think_reflect: Asks the student to devise a procedure for squaring a given triangle, i.e. constructing a square equal in area to it.

sections.title: Area of a Circle
sections.think_reflect: Asks the student why human beings have been so drawn to circular shapes, whether the reasons were purely practical, and what uses the circular shape has been put to.

sections.title: Area of Sector of a Circle

prose_summary: Section 6.1 defines the perimeter of a shape as the total length around its border — the distance a tiny insect would walk in going once round — and recalls the perimeters of a square (4a), an equilateral triangle (3a) and a rectangle (2(a + b)), noting that the square formula is a special case of the rectangle formula; it then observes that the ratio of perimeter to side stays fixed (4:1 for squares, 3:1 for equilateral triangles) however the shape is scaled, and raises the corresponding question for a circle: is the ratio of circumference C to diameter D the same for circles of every size? Section 6.2 introduces this constant as the 'C/D ratio' and explains that its value does not change with the size of the circle, sets a home measurement (winding thread twenty times round a cotton reel) for estimating it, and traces the historical pursuit of the constant now written π — the Mesopotamian value 3 + 1/8, Archimedes' trapping of π between inscribed and circumscribed polygons to give 3 + 10/71 < π < 3 + 1/7, Ptolemy's 377/120, Liu Hui's circle-cutting method, Zu Chongzhi's 22/7 and 355/113, Āryabhaṭa's 3.1416 described as āsanna ('approaching'), Brahmagupta's √10, and finally Mādhava's exact infinite series π/4 = 1 − 1/3 + 1/5 − 1/7 + …, which shifted π from a number to be approximated to a limit to be reached and opened the way to calculus. Section 6.3 explains that π is irrational: unlike the decimal expansions of fractions such as 1/3, 1/11 and 1/7, the digits of π show no repeating pattern, and π cannot be written as a ratio of two integers (a fact proved by Lambert in 1761); it restates the definition of a rational number, stresses that 22/7 is a close-but-not-equal approximation so that one writes π ≈ 22/7 and π ≠ 22/7, and notes that because π is irrational there is no single 'best fraction' for it. Section 6.4 derives the length of a circular arc: from circumference πd = 2πr it uses the reflection symmetry of the circle in a diameter to show that a semicircular arc has length πr, and a quarter-turn rotation to show that a quarter arc has length πr/2; rewriting these as 2πr × 180°/360° and 2πr × 90°/360° it generalises to the arc subtending θ° at the centre, of length 2πr × θ°/360°, and then applies this to a schematic 400 m athletics track (two 84.39 m straights and two semicircles of inner radius 36.5 m, lanes 1.22 m wide) to verify the 400 m circuit and to explain why staggers are needed. Section 6.5 solves a small set of perimeter puzzles: two equal circles each passing through the other's centre, where an equilateral triangle of radii gives 60° angles and hence arcs of one-third of each circumference, totalling 8πr/3; and a comparison of a single large semicircular path with three smaller semicircles on the same segment, where writing each length as π times a radius shows the two paths to be exactly equal. Section 6.6 defines area as the amount of space a plane region occupies, measured relative to a 1 × 1 unit square, and recalls from Grade 8 that a rectangle with sides a and b has area ab square units and a square of side a has area a². Section 6.7 derives the area of a parallelogram by cutting a triangle from one end and reattaching it at the other to form a rectangle with the same base b and height h, giving area = base × height = bh, and then repairs the argument for a 'thin' parallelogram whose perpendicular foot falls outside the base by repeatedly sliding a congruent copy along the base line. Section 6.8 derives the area of a triangle in two ways — by enclosing it in a rectangle of the same base and height, right-angled and obtuse cases treated separately, and more elegantly by fitting two congruent copies together into a parallelogram — arriving at ½ bh, and proves the theorem that a median of a triangle divides it into two triangles of equal area, stressing that the two parts are equal in area although in general not congruent. Section 6.8.1 introduces Heron's formula, which gives the area of a triangle with sides a, b, c as √(s(s−a)(s−b)(s−c)) where s is the semi-perimeter, tests it against the equilateral, isosceles and 3-4-5 triangles by checking each answer against the half-base-times-height formula, mentions the two further area formulas abc/4R and r(a + b + c)/2 involving the circumcircle and incircle, and then presents Brahmagupta's formula √((s−a)(s−b)(s−c)(s−d)) for a cyclic 4-gon — first showing by the example of a rhombus that side lengths alone do not fix a 4-gon's area, verifying the formula for a rectangle and an isosceles trapezium, and finally showing that setting d = 0 reduces it to Heron's formula, so that Brahmagupta's result generalises Heron's. Section 6.9 constructs a square equal in area to a given rectangle, following Baudhāyana's Śhulbasūtra method: mark E on AD with AE = AB, take F the midpoint of ED, draw square AFGH, strike an arc of centre H through A to meet BC at K, and build the square on HP; the construction is shown to be a geometric translation of the identity ((a+b)/2)² − ((a−b)/2)² = ab. Section 6.10 justifies the formula for the area of a circle, first arguing from squares and equilateral triangles that the ratio P² : A depends only on the shape and not on its scale, recounting the Babylonian estimate C²/12 and the Egyptian and Baudhāyana Śhulbasūtra value (8d/9)² = 256r²/81, and then giving Archimedes' result A = πr² obtained from the regular-polygon area ½ × perimeter × inradius as the number of sides grows, together with Nīlakaṇṭha's visual argument in which the circle is cut into ever thinner slices and rearranged into a parallelogram of base πr and height r. Section 6.10.1 defines a sector as the region bounded by an arc and the two radii through its endpoints, uses the reflection and quarter-turn symmetries of the circle to give the semicircular disc ½πr² and the quadrant ¼πr², generalises to the sector subtending θ° at the centre with area πr² × θ/360, and defines a segment as the region bounded by an arc and the chord joining its endpoints.

enumerated_worked_examples.description: Two circles of equal radius r, each passing through the centre of the other; find the perimeter of the shape they form, using the equilateral triangle of radii to show each outer arc is two-thirds of a circumference and obtaining 8πr/3.

Two paths joining P and Q, one a single semicircle and the other three semicircles on sub-segments of PQ; decide which is longer, and show algebraically that because the radii satisfy a' = b' + c' + d' the two paths have equal length.
Apply Heron's formula to an equilateral triangle of side a to obtain (√3/4)a², and check the result against the half-base-times-height formula using the Baudhāyana–Pythagoras theorem.
Apply Heron's formula to an isosceles triangle with equal sides a and base 2b to obtain b√(a² − b²), and verify it against the half-base-times-height formula.

Apply Heron's formula to a triangle with sides 3, 4 and 5 units to obtain area 6 sq. units, and verify it by recognising the triangle as right-angled via the converse of the Baudhāyana–Pythagoras theorem.
Verify Brahmagupta's formula for a rectangle with sides a and b, showing that the formula returns the familiar area ab.

Verify Brahmagupta's formula for an isosceles trapezium with parallel sides 2a and 2b and equal slant sides c, simplifying the surd and matching it with the half-sum-of-parallel-sides times height formula.

enumerated_exercises.description: Given that the perimeter of a circle is 44 cm, find its radius.
Calculate, correct to 3 significant figures, the circumference of a circle with (i) radius 7 cm, (ii) radius 10 cm, (iii) radius 12 cm.
Calculate the length of an arc of a circle when (i) the radius is 3.5 cm and the central angle is 60°, and (ii) the radius is 6.3 m and the central angle is 120°.
Find the perimeter of a sector of a circle of radius 14 cm with sector angle 75°, counting both the curved arc and the two straight radii.
Find the perimeters of nine composite figures (Fig. 6.14 i–ix) built from straight edges together with quarter, half or three-quarter circular arcs.
A car tyre has diameter 56 cm: (i) how far does the car travel in one revolution of the tyre, and (ii) how many revolutions does the tyre make over 10 km?

Find the total perimeter of all the petals in each of two flower figures — (i) arcs centred at the midpoints of the sides of a square of side 14 cm, and (ii) arcs centred at the vertices of a hexagon of side 42 cm.
The ratio of the perimeters of two circles is 5:4; find the ratio of their radii.
Find the area of triangle ADE in Fig. 6.31, given a base of 10 cm and a height of 8 cm from the accompanying figure.
A trapezium has parallel sides 40 cm and 20 cm and equal non-parallel sides of 26 cm each; find its area.
Find the area of a triangle whose sides include 8 cm and 11 cm and whose perimeter is 32 cm.
The sides of a triangular plot are in the ratio 3:5:7 and its perimeter is 300 m; find its area.
One diagonal of a rhombus is twice the other and the rhombus has area 128 cm²; find the length of the shorter diagonal.
ABCD is a parallelogram and P, Q are any two points on side AB; state what can be said about the ratio area(ΔPCD) : area(ΔQCD).
O is any point on the diagonal PR of parallelogram PQRS; prove that triangles PSO and PQO have equal area.
Prove that joining the midpoints of the sides of a 4-gon in order gives a parallelogram whose area is half that of the given 4-gon.
In ΔABC, D is the midpoint of BC and P is any point on median AD; show that area(ΔABP) = area(ΔACP).
P is a point inside square ABCD joined to all four vertices; find the ratio of the combined area of triangles PAB and PCD to the combined area of triangles PBC and PDA.
In ΔABC, D is the midpoint of AB, P is any point on BC and Q lies on AB with CQ parallel to PD; prove that area(ΔBPQ) = ½ area(ΔABC).
Find the area of a sector of a circle of radius 7 cm whose sector angle is 60°.
Find the area of a quadrant of a circle whose circumference is 44 cm.
The minute hand of a clock is 7 cm long; find the area it sweeps in 10 minutes.
A chord of a circle of radius 10 cm subtends 90° at the centre; find the areas of (i) the minor sector subtending 90° and (ii) the major sector subtending 270°, taking π ≈ 3.14.
A chord of a circle of radius 15 cm subtends 60° at the centre; find the areas of the corresponding minor and major segments, taking π ≈ 3.14 and √3 ≈ 1.73.
A car has two non-overlapping wipers, each with a blade of length 28 cm sweeping through 120°; find the total area cleaned in each sweep.
Draw area-model figures corresponding to the identities (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b² and (a + b + c)² = a² + b² + c² + 2ab + 2bc + 2ca, following the given model for (a + b)².
An isosceles triangle has perimeter 40 cm with equal sides of 15 cm each; find its area.
An isosceles triangle has base 10 cm and area 60 cm²; find the lengths of its equal sides.
A right-angled triangle has area 54 sq. cm and one leg of length 12 cm; find its perimeter.
The sides of a triangle are in the ratio 2:3:4 and its perimeter is 45 cm; find its area.
A triangle has sides 7 cm, 24 cm and 25 cm; find its area in two different ways.
A bicycle wheel has diameter 60 cm; find how far the cyclist has travelled after the wheel has rotated 100 times.
Find the area of a quadrant of a circle whose circumference is 66 cm.
A car wheel has outer radius 28 cm; calculate the distance travelled in one complete turn and the number of turns made over a journey of 1 km.
Using the base-times-height formula for a parallelogram and the given figure, show that the area of a trapezium is ½(a + b)h.
By dividing a trapezium into two triangles, show that its area is half the sum of the parallel sides multiplied by the height.
Show how two identical copies of a trapezium can be fitted together to make a parallelogram, and explain how this yields the formula for the area of a trapezium.
Show that the area of a kite is half the product of its diagonals, (i) using algebra and (ii) using geometry.

Three problems on fitting congruent shapes: (i) show a rectangle with sides 2a, 2b has four times the area of one with sides a, b and test whether four copies fit; (ii) show a triangle with sides 2a, 2b, 2c has four times the area of one with sides a, b, c and test whether four copies fit; (iii) show a triangle with sides 3a, 3b, 3c has nine times the area and test whether nine copies fit.
Find what fraction of each of two rectangles (Fig. 6.45 and Fig. 6.46) is covered by the circles packed inside it.
Make a conjecture about the area occupied by circles fitted into a rectangle in the manner shown, test it for 10, 20 and 50 circles, and then prove it.
